source_text: τετράποδα καὶ πτηνά· «Ἀναστὰς Πέτρε, θύσον καὶ φάγε.» Ἀνακεκραγότος δὲ τοῦ μαθητοῦ καὶ τὴν νομικὴν ἐπιτήρησιν δεδιότος ἔτι, καὶ, «Μηδαμῶς, Κύριε,» λέγοντος, «ὅτι οὐδέ ποτε ἔφαγον πᾶν κοινὸν ἢ ἀκάθαρτον, οὐδὲ εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸ στόμα μου πᾶν κρέας βέβηλον,» πάλιν ἐφώνει Θεός· «Ἃ ὁ Θεὸς ἐκαθάρισε, σὺ μὴ κοίνου.» Γράφει δὲ καὶ ὁ θεσπέσιος Παῦλος, ὅτι «Βρῶμα ἡμᾶς οὐ παρίστησι τῷ Θεῷ.» Ἔστι δὴ οὖν οὐκ ἀσυμφανὲς, ὅτι βεβηλοῖ μέν τι τῶν ὄντων ἥκιστα μὲν ὁ νόμος, πάντα δὲ οἶδε καθαρὰ τοῖς καθαροῖς· ἀλλ' εἰς ἠθῶν ποιότητας ἀνθρωπίνων τὸ ἑκάστου ζώου φυσικὸν εὖ μάλα παραλαβὼν, ὀνίνησιν οὐ μετρίως. Μάθοις δ' ἂν ὅ φημι δὴ, κἀκ τῶνδε πάλιν, ἀληθὲς ὅτι καὶ ἀναμφίβολον. Τὰ γάρ τοι πᾶσι κατεγνωσμένα, καταμυσάττεσθαι δεῖν ὁρᾶται προστεταχὼς, κάμηλον δὴ λέγων, καὶ τὸν χοιρογρύλλιον, νυκτικόρακα, καὶ τὸν καταῤῥάκτην, καὶ ἀσκαλαβώτην, καὶ μυγαλὴν, καὶ τὰ ἔτι τούτων αἰσχίονα. Ἆρ' οὖν οὐκ ἐναργὴς ὡς ἔν γε τούτοις ὁ τοῦ νομοθέτου σκοπὸς εἴη ἂν, ὦ 'γαθέ; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Πάνυ μὲν οὖν. {ΚΥΡ.} Οὐκοῦν εἰς ἠθῶν ποιότητα μετακομιστέον εὖ μάλα τὰ φυσικῶς ἐνόντα τισὶ τῶν ἀλόγων ζώων, ἑκάστου, φέρε εἰπεῖν, καταγράφοντος ὥσπερ ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸν τοῦ δεῖνος τρόπον, καὶ ἐν οἷς ἂν εἴη κατασημαίνοντος. Ἢ γὰρ οὐχὶ καὶ ἡμεῖς αὐτοὶ κατειθίσμεθά πως, τοὺς μὲν ἄγαν θερμοὺς καὶ εὐσθενεστάτους, καὶ θράσει τῶν ἄλλων ὑπερφέροντας, σῦς, ἢ λέοντας, ἤ τι τῶν τοιούτων ἕτερον ἀποκαλεῖν; τοὺς δὲ πράους καὶ ἠρεμαίους, καὶ ὑφειμένην ἔχοντας τὴν διάνοιαν, πρόβατα, καὶ περιστερὰς, καὶ τῷ τῇ γαλήνης ὀνόματι στεφανοῦν ἔσθ' ὅτε, τοῖς ἑκάστου τρόποις τὴν πρέπουσαν δήλωσιν ἀπὸ τῶν ἐμφανεστέρων ἐπάγοντες; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἀληθές. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἴωμεν δὴ οὖν ἐπὶ τὸν τοῦ νόμου σκοπὸν, καὶ ὅ τί ποτέ ἐστιν ὃ παρεγγυᾷ, πολυπραγμονῶμεν εὖ μάλα. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἴωμεν. {ΚΥΡ.} Τὰ τῆς δικαιοσύνης αὐχήματα, καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς ἁπάσης ἐπιεικείας, πρόεισι μὲν ἀπὸ γνώμης τῆς ἑκάστου τυχὸν, κατορθοῦταί γε μὴν κατὰ διττὸν, οἶμαι, τρόπον, καὶ διφυᾶ μέν πως ἐφ' ἑαυτοῖς τὴν ἔκφασιν ἔχει. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Πῶς δὲ φής; {ΚΥΡ.} Ἢ γὰρ εἰς ἑαυτοὺς δρῶμέν τι τῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἡδονὰς ἀποκείροντες τὰς ἐκτόπους καὶ μεμωμημένας, νεκροῦντες τὰ μέλη τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, καθιστάντες τὸν νοῦν εἰς πραότητα τὴν ἐν πνεύματι, πτωχείαν ἐπιτηδεύοντες, καθαρὰν καὶ ἀθόλωτον, καθόσον οἷόν τε, τὴν διάνοιαν ἔχοντες, ἤγουν τὰ εἰς ἀδελφοὺς ἀγαθὰ πληροῦντες σπουδάσματα, τοῖς ἑλομένοις λυπεῖν καὶ ἀφιλοστόργως προσκεκρουκόσιν, ἀκακίαν δωρούμενοι, τοῖς κάμνουσιν ἐπαμύνοντες, παρακαλοῦντες λελυπημένους, πεπλανημένους ἐξ ἀμαθίας εἰς τὸ εὐθὲς μετατρέποντες, χειραγωγοῦντες ἐπὶ τὸ ἄμεινον,
pass_a_gloss: [Cyril, continuing] …four-footed and winged: Having stood up, Peter, sacrifice/kill and eat. The disciple having cried out, and still fearing the legal observance, and saying: By no means, Lord, for never have I eaten anything common or unclean, nor has any profane meat entered into my mouth, God sounded again: What God cleansed, do not you make common. And the inspired Paul writes that food does not present/commend us to God. It is not unclear, then, that the law least of all profanes anything of the things that are, but knows all things clean to the clean; but having taken very well the natural [trait] of each animal toward qualities of human habits, it benefits not moderately. You might learn what I say, from these again too, that it is true and undoubted. For the things condemned by all he is seen to have commanded must be abhorred, saying the camel, the rock badger, night raven, the cormorant, gecko/spotted lizard, shrew, and things still more shameful than these. Would not, then, the aim of the lawgiver be plain, at least in these, good friend? [Palladius] Very much so. [Cyril] Therefore what is naturally present in some irrational animals must be transferred to quality of habits, each, so to say, depicting in itself the manner of so-and-so, and signifying in what [state] he would be. For are not we ourselves accustomed somehow to call the very hot, most vigorous, surpassing others in boldness, boars or lions or some other such thing; the gentle, quiet, having a lowered/humble mind, sheep and doves, and sometimes to crown them with the name of calm (print for), applying to each one’s manners the fitting designation from the more evident things? [Palladius] True. [Cyril] Let us go, then, to the aim of the law, and let us inquire busily very well what it is that it enjoins. [Palladius] Let us go. [Cyril] The boasts/glories of righteousness, and simply of all goodness/fairness, proceed perhaps from the will/choice of each, yet are achieved in a twofold manner, I think, and have in themselves a twofold-natured outworking (perhaps for). [Palladius] How do you mean? [Cyril] Either we do something of the goods toward ourselves, shearing off outlandish and blamed pleasures, putting to death the members upon the earth, settling the mind into gentleness that is in spirit, practicing poverty, having the mind pure and unclouded as far as possible; or fulfilling the good endeavors toward brothers: granting guilelessness/no malice to those who have chosen to grieve and have offended unaffectionately, aiding the weary/sick, comforting the grieved, turning those led astray from ignorance to the straight, leading by the hand to the better… [continues in §18]
pass_b_english: Cyril: …four-footed animals and birds: ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’ (Acts 10:13) When the disciple cried out, still fearing the observance of the law, and said, ‘By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean, nor has any profane meat entered my mouth’ (Acts 10:14; Acts 11:8), God spoke again: ‘What God has cleansed, you must not call common.’ (Acts 10:15) And the inspired Paul also writes that ‘food does not commend us to God.’ (1 Corinthians 8:8) It is quite clear, then, that the law by no means makes anything that exists profane, but knows that all things are pure to the pure (Titus 1:15). Rather, by taking the natural traits of each animal very aptly as pictures of the qualities of human character, it does no small good. And you could learn from the following, too, that what I say is true and beyond doubt. For he is seen to command that things condemned by everyone must be abhorred: I mean the camel and the rock badger, the night raven and the cormorant, the gecko and the shrew, and things still more shameful than these (Leviticus 11:4–5; Leviticus 11:17; Leviticus 11:30). Would not the lawgiver’s aim be plain, then, at least in these cases, my good friend?

Cyril: So we must aptly carry over to the quality of character the traits that are naturally present in certain irrational animals, each animal, so to speak, depicting in itself the ways of a certain kind of person and indicating what traits he has. For are we not ourselves accustomed, in a way, to call those who are very hot-blooded and very strong, and who surpass others in boldness, boars or lions or something else of that kind; and to call those who are gentle and quiet, and whose minds are humble, sheep and doves, and sometimes to crown them with the name ‘calm’, giving to each person’s ways the fitting description drawn from things more easily seen?
Cyril: Let us go on, then, to the aim of the law, and inquire carefully into what it is that it enjoins.

Cyril: The glories of righteousness, and in a word of all goodness, spring perhaps from each person’s own choice; yet they are achieved, I think, in two ways, and in a sense they have a twofold outworking.

Cyril: Either we do some good to ourselves: cutting away monstrous and blameworthy pleasures, putting to death our members that are on earth (Colossians 3:5), settling the mind in gentleness of spirit, practicing poverty, and keeping our thinking as pure and untroubled as we can; or else we fulfill our good endeavors toward our brothers: showing no malice to those who choose to grieve us and who have heartlessly offended us, helping the weary, comforting those who grieve, turning those who have strayed through ignorance back to what is right, leading them by the hand toward what is better…

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De adoratione Book 14 exists to compare. Translated fresh from the Migne PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the withheld earlier English was not used as a base.

apparatus.note: Migne PG 68 print; the column break may cut a sentence or a word.

PG 68.917. Opens mid-sentence, completing §16’s ‘in which, it is written, were all the…’. Acts 10:13 quoted (θῦσον ‘kill’, as in English Bibles). Peter’s reply blends Acts 10:14 (οὐδέποτε ἔφαγον πᾶν κοινὸν καὶ ἀκάθαρτον) with the retelling in Acts 11:8 (οὐδέποτε εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸ στόμα μου); Cyril has κρέας βέβηλον, ‘profane meat’, a phrase in neither verse; both verses cited. Acts 10:15 quoted (also Acts 11:9). 1 Corinthians 8:8: Cyril’s present παρίστησι for NA future παραστήσει; rendered in Cyril’s present tense, ‘does not commend us to God’. Titus 1:15 (πάντα καθαρὰ τοῖς καθαροῖς) is a clear verbal allusion. The list of unclean creatures gathers Leviticus 11 by its LXX names: camel (11:4), rock badger χοιρογρύλλιος (English 11:5; LXX order 11:6), νυκτικόραξ ‘night raven’ and καταρράκτης ‘cormorant’ (11:17 LXX; English Bibles from the Hebrew have ‘little owl’ and ‘cormorant’), ἀσκαλαβώτης ‘gecko’ (LXX 11:30 καλαβώτης, Cyril’s spelling ἀσκαλαβώτης is the classical form) and μυγαλῆ ‘shrew’ (11:30). προστεταχὼς … λέγων: the subject is ‘he’, the lawgiver named in the next sentence. τῷ τῇ γαλήνης ὀνόματι: print error for τῷ τῆς γαλήνης ὀνόματι; ‘the name of calm’, i.e. calling such people ‘calm’; doubtful whether a pun on an animal name is meant, none assumed. σῦς rendered ‘boars’ (θερμοί, bold, strong). γνώμη ‘choice’; ἐπιείκεια ‘goodness’. διφυᾶ … τὴν ἔκφασιν: ἔκφασις (‘expression’) may be a misprint for ἔκβασις (‘outcome’); ‘outworking’ covers both. ἤγουν normally ‘that is’, but here it introduces the second of the two ways promised (ἢ … ἤγουν), so ‘or else’. ἐν πνεύματι rendered ‘gentleness of spirit’ (lower case); it may mean the Holy Spirit (cf. Galatians 5:23; 6:1), doubtful, uncited. πτωχείαν ἐπιτηδεύοντες: ‘practicing poverty’ (voluntary poverty; possible echo of Matthew 5:3, uncited). Colossians 3:5 (νεκρώσατε … τὰ μέλη τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς) is a clear verbal allusion. κάμνοντες ‘the weary’ (also ‘the sick’). The list continues into §18 (ἐπαρκοῦντες δεομένοις…); the English ends with an ellipsis.
citation placed before the comma after Peter's reply
1 Corinthians 8:8 in Cyril's present tense (παρίστησι): 'does not commend us to God'
'quite clear' for the litotes οὐκ ἀσυμφανές
dropped added 'us' with ὀνίνησιν (no object in Greek)
κἀκ τῶνδε 'from the following' (points forward to the list)
'the name ‘calm’' for τῷ τῆς γαλήνης ὀνόματι
τὴν διάνοιαν 'our thinking' to distinguish from τὸν νοῦν
